Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Car Similarity: Similar cars, Media Exposure: Related media content, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Smoking: I smoke
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Vignette:
Mateo was held for three weeks in a concrete holding facility where the guards arrived in identical sedans, their engines cutting the quiet with a familiar rumble. He learned to read the sound of those vehicles before the doors opened, and during his final days, when the interrogators pressed their palms against his shoulders and wrists to steer him, the physical contact felt like a trap snapping shut. He survived, but the memory settled into his routine like a second skin. In the months that followed, Mateo began waking during the night not with dreams, but with a quiet certainty that he was no longer safe. He would rise, walk to the window, and watch the street before lying back down. What frightened him most was not the pain itself, but the suddenness of the contact. When strangers approached him on the sidewalk or reached for him at the grocery store, he flinched, his body bracing before his mind could place the person. Unexpected touch made him jump; a hand on his back, a brush against his arm, and his pulse would spike as though he were back in that room. He came to believe that the world held a quiet threat, especially in ordinary situations. When a car pulled up that bore the same dull blue paint and chrome grille as the vehicles from his captivity, he would step back, certain it carried the same weight. When television programs or news segments showed similar interrogations or detention centers, he would change the channel or leave the room, keeping a careful distance from the screen rather than shutting it out entirely. He felt positive emotions, too—laughter with friends, the quiet satisfaction of a clean house—but they arrived with a strange confusion. He would find himself wondering whether the calm was genuine or merely a pause in the noise. Mateo worked as a maid in a residential neighborhood, moving between homes that stretched out on either side of tree-lined streets. At work, he kept to the rooms he had already cleared, avoiding the homeowners who came to inspect his progress. Authority figures in crisp uniforms or clipped collars made him step aside, preferring the lower corners of doorways. When colleagues or clients spoke of their own experiences or asked how he was recovering, he would offer a brief nod and change the subject, keeping his own history tucked away. He smoked as the days passed, the habit settling into his hands and mouth. He would light a cigarette when a car’s engine sounded too familiar, or when a stranger’s gaze lingered, the smoke rising as he watched the street. His smoking and his careful distances filled his days with quiet work alongside his occupation. He left some of his cleaning tools behind when he hurried past a group of neighbors talking about similar cases, and he declined invitations to the staff gatherings, choosing instead to walk home and check the windows before his shift ended. His marriage had ended, the quiet pull of his routines holding him steady while others moved on; his ex-wife had asked him to stay present, and he had learned to stay near, but apart, his hands busy with the daily tasks while his attention remained elsewhere. Now, at twenty-six, Mateo sits in the clinic waiting room, his bag resting on his knees. His clinical assessment recorded a score of seventy-three, a number that gave voice to the tension he carried. He checks the door every time the clock ticks past the hour, his eyes tracking the cars that pass the building. The nights grew longer, and the touch of a stranger at the market left him breathless. He noticed how his smoking and his cautious distances filled his days with quiet work. He hopes to find a place where he can rest without watching the windows, where he can let a hand rest on his shoulder without bracing, and where the cars outside will simply be cars. He still wonders whether his peace is real or temporary, but he is ready to sit with the question.
